Magnetic Filters Compared with Other Filters | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Magnetic Filters Compared with Other Filters

Most industrial filters work by blocking. The fluid passes through a mesh, a paper, a bag or a cartridge, and the particles are held back. A magnetic filter works by attraction. The fluid passes over magnets, and iron particles are pulled out of the flow and held on the magnet surface.
This guide compares the two approaches for coolants, oils, wash liquids and process fluids.
How a magnetic filter works

A magnetic filter is a housing fitted into a pipeline. Inside are one or more high strength magnetic rods. Fluid enters, passes over and around the rods, and leaves. Iron and steel particles in the fluid are drawn to the rods and held there.
A SMAG inline magnetic liquid trap.
The rods are cleaned by lifting them out of the housing and wiping off the collected material. Nothing is consumed. The magnets keep their strength for many years.
What each type catches

{1}Bag, cartridge and paper filters{/1} catch anything larger than their pore size. They catch iron, aluminium, plastic, dirt and fibres alike. They cannot catch anything smaller than the pore size, and a very fine filter blocks quickly and restricts the flow.
{1}Magnetic filters{/1} catch iron and steel of any size, down to particles of a few microns, with no restriction to the flow. They do not catch aluminium, brass, plastic or dirt.
In practice, most contamination in a metalworking or steel processing fluid is iron. A magnetic filter removes that, and a coarser barrier filter handles the rest.

Where a magnetic filter helps most

{1}Grinding and machining coolant.{/1} Fine steel swarf shortens coolant life, blocks nozzles, scores machine slideways and marks the finished surface. A magnetic filter removes it before it circulates, so the coolant lasts longer and the finish improves.
{1}Hydraulic and lubricating oil.{/1} Wear particles from pumps, gears and bearings are mostly iron. Removing them slows further wear.
{1}Wash and rinse liquids.{/1} Iron particles from washed parts build up in the tank and are redeposited on the next batch.
{1}Process fluids in steel and pipeline systems.{/1} Rust, scale and black powder are iron compounds and are held by a magnet.
Where a barrier filter is still needed

Non-magnetic contamination needs a barrier. Aluminium and brass swarf, plastic, fibres and general dirt pass over a magnet. In a system with mixed contamination, fit the magnetic filter first. It removes the bulk of the load, so the barrier filter downstream lasts far longer and can be coarser.
Sizing a magnetic filter
Three things decide the size:
{1}Flow rate.{/1} The fluid must spend enough time near the rods for particles to be drawn out. A larger housing for a higher flow.
{1}Contamination load.{/1} More iron means more rods, or more frequent cleaning.
{1}Particle size.{/1} Fine particles need higher strength rods. SMAG rods are made up to 13,500 gauss.

Preventing Product Recalls in the Food Industry | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Preventing Product Recalls in the Food Industry

A product recall is one of the most costly events a food business can face. The product must be traced, collected and destroyed. Sales stop. Retailers lose confidence. The story may reach the press. Recovery can take years.
Many recalls are avoidable. This guide looks at the common causes and the controls that prevent them, with a focus on metal.
Why food is recalled
The main reasons for food recalls are:
{1}Undeclared allergens{/1}, such as milk, nuts or gluten missing from the label.
{1}Microbiological contamination{/1}, such as salmonella or listeria.
{1}Physical contamination{/1}, mostly metal, glass and plastic.
Labelling and packaging errors.
{1}Chemical contamination{/1}, such as cleaning agents or excess additives.
Physical contamination is the category where engineering controls do most of the work. Metal is the largest part of it.
What a recall costs

The direct costs are the product, the logistics of collecting it, disposal, and the staff time spent managing the event. The indirect costs are larger. Lost sales during and after the recall, penalties from retailers, legal claims, higher insurance and the long term damage to the brand.
A single high strength magnetic separator costs a small fraction of a single recall.
Control 1: know your hazards

Under HACCP, every plant must list the hazards at each stage and decide where they must be controlled. For metal, walk the line and write down where iron and steel can enter. Raw materials, sieves, mills, mixers, pumps, conveyors and maintenance work are the usual sources. See our guide on {1}critical control points{/1}
Control 2: remove metal at every stage

Fit a magnetic separator at intake, after each stage that sheds metal, and before packing. Use a grid or grate for powders in a hopper, a drawer housing for enclosed lines, a liquid trap for pipelines and a plate or chute magnet for deep beds.
A SMAG housed liquid trap for syrup, oil and sauce lines.

The final separator before packing is the last chance to catch a fragment. Use the highest practical strength here. SMAG rods are made up to 13,500 gauss, which holds fine particles and work hardened stainless steel as well as ordinary iron.
Control 3: cover the metals a magnet passes

Aluminium, copper, brass and some stainless grades are passed by a magnet. If these are a risk on your line, add a metal detector after the final magnet. The magnet removes the bulk of the contamination and protects the detector from constant rejects. The detector catches the remainder.
Control 4: prove the controls work
An auditor wants evidence. For each separator, keep:
The {1}tested certificate of magnetic strength{/1} supplied when it was made.
A {1}cleaning log{/1} showing when it was cleaned and what was found.
{1}Gauss meter readings{/1} taken at least once a year, compared with the certificate.
An {1}inspection record{/1} for tube damage, seal wear and loose fixings.
A separator with no records is treated as no control at all.
Control 5: manage change

Recalls often follow a change. A new supplier, a new product, a repair or a new machine. Review the hazard list and the separator positions every time the line changes, and after every metal complaint, even if the complaint is not confirmed.
Control 6: train the people

Operators must know how to clean a separator, what to record, and what to do when they find more metal than usual. Maintenance staff must know to count tools and fixings, and to clean with a hand magnet before a restart.

Reducing Metal Contamination in Food Processing | Santosh Magnetic Works
{1}Guides{/1} / Reducing Metal Contamination in Food Processing

Metal in food is a serious hazard. A single fragment can injure a customer, trigger a recall and damage a brand for years. Most of that metal is iron or steel, and most of it can be removed with magnets.
This guide gives the practical steps that reduce the risk.
Where the metal comes from
Metal enters a food line in three ways.

{1}It arrives with the raw material.{/1} Grain, sugar, flour, salt, spices, cocoa and dried fruit come from farms, mills and warehouses. Along the way they pick up nails, wire, staples, rust and pieces of broken equipment.

{1}The line makes it.{/1} Every moving part wears. Mill blades, sieve mesh, mixer paddles, pump rotors, conveyor chains and bearings shed particles as they run. Stainless steel equipment sheds stainless particles.
{1}People bring it.{/1} Dropped fixings after maintenance, a broken blade, swarf from a repair, a paperclip or a pen spring.
What it costs

A recall in the food industry costs far more than the product itself. There is the cost of finding and collecting the product, the lost sales, the legal exposure and the loss of trust from retailers and consumers. Metal is one of the most common causes of recalls worldwide.
Retailer audits treat metal control as a basic requirement. A line with no magnetic protection, or with separators that are never checked, will fail.
